expectedText:
CLIENT EMPLOYER / LABOR CONTRACTOR LIABILITY (LABOR CODE § 2810.3) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS CLIENT EMPLOYER / LABOR CONTRACTOR LIABILITY INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California Labor Code Section 2810.3, which addresses civil legal responsibility between a "client employer" that obtains workers through a "labor contractor" (such as a staffing agency or temporary services provider) and that labor contractor. Acme, Inc. has described its use of labor contractors as follows: We use a staffing agency to supply approximately 20 warehouse workers. This document states the content of the statute; it does not determine whether Section 2810.3 applies to any particular arrangement, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

DEFINITIONS: "CLIENT EMPLOYER" AND "LABOR CONTRACTOR"
California Labor Code Section 2810.3 defines a "client employer" as a business entity, regardless of its form, that obtains or is provided workers to perform labor within its usual course of business from a labor contractor. A "labor contractor" is defined as an individual or entity that supplies, with or without a contract, a client employer with workers to perform labor within the client employer's usual course of business. "Usual course of business" means the regular and customary work of a business, performed within or upon the premises or worksite of the client employer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Client employer” means a business entity, regardless of its form, that obtains or is provided workers to perform labor within its usual course of business from a labor contractor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(1)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of "client employer" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "“Labor contractor” means an individual or entity that supplies, either with or without a contract, a client employer with workers to perform labor within the client employer’s usual course of business."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of "labor contractor" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "“Usual course of business” means the regular and customary work of a business, performed within or upon the premises or worksite of the client employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(6) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of "usual course of business" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  Known gap: The statute's definitions of "labor," "wages," and "worker" incorporate other Labor Code sections (Section 200 and the Industrial Welfare Commission's overtime-exemption wage orders under Section 515) by reference rather than restating them, so a full determination of who counts as a covered "worker" can require consulting those other provisions.

SIZE THRESHOLDS AND DEFINITIONAL EXCLUSIONS
Section 2810.3 excludes certain entities from its definitions entirely, which removes them from the statute's liability-sharing scheme. A business entity is not a "client employer" if its total workforce (including workers hired directly and those obtained from any labor contractor) numbers fewer than 25, or if it has five or fewer workers supplied by a labor contractor or labor contractors at any given time. The state and any political subdivision of the state, including a city, county, city and county, or special district, are also excluded from the "client employer" definition. Separately, the term "labor contractor" does not include a bona fide nonprofit community-based organization that provides services to workers; a bona fide labor organization, apprenticeship program, or hiring hall operated under a collective bargaining agreement; a motion picture payroll services company as defined by reference to the Unemployment Insurance Code; or a third party to a qualifying employee leasing arrangement (as defined by a specified 1995 workers' compensation experience rating plan rule, as that rule read on January 1, 2014) where the arrangement contractually obligates the client employer to assume all civil legal responsibility and liability under the statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A business entity with a workforce of fewer than 25 workers, including those hired directly by the client employer and those obtained from, or provided by, any labor contractor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(1)(B)(i) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, workforce-size exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "A business entity with five or fewer workers supplied by a labor contractor or labor contractors to the client employer at any given time."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(1)(B)(ii) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, five-or-fewer-supplied-workers exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "The state or any political subdivision of the state, including any city, county, city and county, or special district."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(1)(B)(iii) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, state/political-subdivision exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "A bona fide nonprofit, community-based organization that provides services to workers."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(3)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, nonprofit community-based organization exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "A bona fide labor organization or apprenticeship program or hiring hall operated pursuant to a collective bargaining agreement."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(3)(B) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, labor organization/hiring hall exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "A motion picture payroll services company, as defined in subparagraph (A) of paragraph (4) of subdivision (f) of Section 679 of the Unemployment Insurance Code."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(3)(C) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, motion picture payroll services company exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "A third party who is a party to an employee leasing arrangement, as defined by Rule 4 of Section V of the California Workers’ Compensation Experience Rating Plan-1995 (Section 2353.1 of Title 10 of the California Code of Regulations), as it read on January 1, 2014, except those arrangements described in subrule d of Rule 4 of Section V, if the employee leasing arrangement contractually obligates the client employer to assume all civil legal responsibility and civil liability under this act."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(a)(3)(D) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, employee leasing arrangement exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  Known gap: These are two distinct exclusion lists: one narrows who counts as a "client employer" (the workforce-size and public-entity exclusions), and the other narrows who counts as a "labor contractor" (the nonprofit, labor-organization, motion-picture-payroll, and employee-leasing exclusions). The statute does not contain a separately labeled exclusion for "small businesses" as such, for motor carriers as a category, or for unionized construction generally beyond the labor-organization/hiring-hall and collective-bargaining language quoted above; whether a given arrangement fits one of the statute's specific exclusions is a fact-specific determination this sheet does not make.

SCOPE OF SHARED CIVIL LIABILITY
Where Section 2810.3 applies, a client employer shares with its labor contractor all civil legal responsibility and civil liability, as to workers supplied by that labor contractor, for the payment of wages and for any failure to secure valid workers' compensation coverage as required by Labor Code Section 3700. This shared liability applies even where the client employer is not otherwise the workers' direct employer for purposes of separate wage-payment statutes. Section 2810.3 separately provides that a client employer may not shift to its labor contractor any legal duties or liabilities arising under Division 5 of the Labor Code (the occupational safety and health provisions commencing with Section 6300) with respect to workers the labor contractor supplies -- meaning the client employer retains those duties itself rather than sharing or delegating them. The statute states that this liability-sharing and non-delegation scheme is in addition to, and supplemental of, any other theories of liability or requirement established by other statutes or the common law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A client employer shall share with a labor contractor all civil legal responsibility and civil liability for all workers supplied by that labor contractor for both of the following:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, shared liability for wages and workers' compensation coverage (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "The payment of wages."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, wage payment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "Failure to secure valid workers’ compensation coverage as required by Section 3700."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, workers' compensation coverage (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "A client employer shall not shift to the labor contractor any legal duties or liabilities under Division 5 (commencing with Section 6300) with respect to workers supplied by the labor contractor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, non-delegable occupational safety and health duties (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "The provisions of subdivisions (b) and (c) are in addition to, and shall be supplemental of, any other theories of liability or requirement established by statute or common law."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(f) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, cumulative with other liability theories (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "Thus, even if the business entity is not the wage claimant’s employer, and therefore owes
no duty to pay wages under section 1194, the entity is nonetheless liable because section
2810.3 imposes joint liability."
  — Noe v. Superior Court (2015) 237 Cal.App.4th 316, California Court of Appeal, describing Section 2810.3's joint-liability effect (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2804850/noe-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: Section 2810.3 itself addresses wage payment, workers' compensation coverage, and occupational safety and health duties; it does not, by its own text, create shared liability for other types of claims (such as anti-discrimination or retaliation claims brought under different statutes), and this sheet does not address whether or how other statutes might separately extend liability to a client employer for those other claim types.

ADDITIONAL LIABILITY CARVE-OUTS FOR SPECIFIC BUSINESS CATEGORIES
Beyond the definitional exclusions, Section 2810.3 states that it does not impose individual liability on a homeowner for labor or services received at the home, or on the owner of a home-based business for labor or services received at the home. It also does not impose liability on a client employer for its use of an independent contractor other than a labor contractor, and does not change the definition of independent contractor. The statute further states that it does not impose liability on several specific categories of arrangements, including a client employer that is not a motor carrier of property, based solely on its use of a third-party motor carrier with interstate or intrastate operating authority to ship or receive freight; a motor carrier of property subcontracting with another motor carrier using the other carrier's own employees and vehicles; a client employer that is not a household mover, based solely on its use of a permitted third-party household mover; a permitted household mover subcontracting with another permitted mover using the other mover's own employees and vehicles; a cable operator, direct-to-home satellite service provider, or telephone corporation contracting with a company to build, install, maintain, or repair using that company's own employees and vehicles where the contractor's name is visible on uniforms and vehicles; and a motor club contracting with a third party to provide motor club services using that third party's own employees and vehicles where the contractor's name is visible on its vehicles.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This section does not impose individual liability on a homeowner for labor or services received at the home or the owner of a home-based business for labor or services received at the home."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(n) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, homeowner and home-based business exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "This section does not impose liability on a client employer for the use of an independent contractor other than a labor contractor or to change the definition of independent contractor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(o) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, independent contractor exclusion (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "This section does not impose liability on the following:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(p) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, introductory clause to specific-category carve-outs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "A client employer that is not a motor carrier of property based solely on the employer’s use of a third-party motor carrier of property with interstate or intrastate operating authority to ship or receive freight."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(p)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, motor carrier of property carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "A client employer that is a cable operator, as defined by Section 5830 of the Public Utilities Code, a direct-to-home satellite service provider, or a telephone corporation, as defined by Section 234 of the Public Utilities Code, based upon its contracting with a company to build, install, maintain, or perform repair work utilizing the employees and vehicles of the contractor if the name of the contractor is visible on employee uniforms and vehicles."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(p)(5) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, cable/satellite/telephone corporation carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  Known gap: This clause paraphrases the motor-carrier, household-mover, cable/satellite/telephone, and motor-club categories in subdivision (p); only the introductory language and the motor-carrier and cable/telephone-corporation examples are reproduced as exact quotations below. Each of these carve-outs has its own specific conditions (for example, the contractor's name being visible on uniforms or vehicles) that determine whether it applies to a given arrangement.

NOTICE, ENFORCEMENT, AND ANTI-RETALIATION
Before filing a civil action against a client employer for violations covered by Section 2810.3, a worker or the worker's representative must, at least 30 days beforehand, notify the client employer of the violations described in subdivision (b) (the wage-payment and workers' compensation coverage provisions). Neither the client employer nor the labor contractor may take adverse action against a worker for providing that notification or for filing a claim or civil action. Separately, upon request by a state enforcement agency or department, a client employer or labor contractor must provide the agency or department with information within its possession, custody, or control that is required to verify compliance with applicable state laws, and must make records available promptly for inspection and copying. The statute authorizes the Labor Commissioner, the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, and the Employment Development Department each to adopt regulations and rules of practice and procedure to administer and enforce the provisions within their respective jurisdictions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "At least 30 days prior to filing a civil action against a client employer for violations covered by this section, a worker or the worker’s representative shall notify the client employer of violations under subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, 30-day pre-filing notice requirement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "Neither the client employer nor the labor contractor may take any adverse action against any worker for providing notification of violations or filing a claim or civil action."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, anti-retaliation provision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "Upon request by a state enforcement agency or department, a client employer or a labor contractor shall provide to the agency or department any information within its possession, custody, or control required to verify compliance with applicable state laws."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(i) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, information requests by state enforcement agencies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  Known gap: These citations are to different subdivisions of the same statute (Section 2810.3) rather than independent sources. This clause does not describe any implementing regulations the Labor Commissioner, the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, or the Employment Development Department may have adopted under their respective enforcement authority, and does not address the required contents or method of the 30-day pre-filing notice.

CONTRACTUAL REMEDIES BETWEEN THE PARTIES AND ANTI-WAIVER RULE
Section 2810.3 does not prohibit a client employer from establishing, exercising, or enforcing by contract any otherwise lawful remedies against a labor contractor for liability created by the labor contractor's acts, and it does not prohibit a labor contractor from doing the same against a client employer for liability created by the client employer's acts. This preserves the parties' ability to allocate responsibility between themselves by contract (for example, through indemnification provisions), separate from the liability-sharing the statute itself imposes toward workers. The statute also provides that a waiver of Section 2810.3 is contrary to public policy and is void and unenforceable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This section does not prohibit a client employer from establishing, exercising, or enforcing by contract any otherwise lawful remedies against a labor contractor for liability created by acts of a labor contractor."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(g) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, client employer's contractual remedies against labor contractor preserved (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "This section does not prohibit a labor contractor from establishing, exercising, or enforcing by contract any otherwise lawful remedies against a client employer for liability created by acts of a client employer."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(h) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, labor contractor's contractual remedies against client employer preserved (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  "A waiver of this section is contrary to public policy, and is void and unenforceable."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(m) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, anti-waiver provision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2810.3.)
  Known gap: These citations are to different subdivisions of the same statute (Section 2810.3) rather than independent sources. This clause states that the statute preserves the parties' ability to allocate responsibility between themselves by contract; it does not describe how any particular indemnification provision should be drafted or would be interpreted, and does not address whether a specific contractual term between a given client employer and labor contractor is enforceable.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet regarding California Labor Code Section 2810.3 was prepared by Jordan T. Reyes for Acme, Inc. and reviewed in Oakland, California on September 1, 2026. It reflects the statutory text as of the date checked above and does not reflect any amendments made after that date.

citations.quote: A client employer that is not a motor carrier of property based solely on the employer’s use of a third-party motor carrier of property with interstate or intrastate operating authority to ship or receive freight.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(p)(5) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, cable/satellite/telephone corporation carve-out
citations.quote: A client employer that is a cable operator, as defined by Section 5830 of the Public Utilities Code, a direct-to-home satellite service provider, or a telephone corporation, as defined by Section 234 of the Public Utilities Code, based upon its contracting with a company to build, install, maintain, or perform repair work utilizing the employees and vehicles of the contractor if the name of the contractor is visible on employee uniforms and vehicles.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause paraphrases the motor-carrier, household-mover, cable/satellite/telephone, and motor-club categories in subdivision (p); only the introductory language and the motor-carrier and cable/telephone-corporation examples are reproduced as exact quotations below. Each of these carve-outs has its own specific conditions (for example, the contractor's name being visible on uniforms or vehicles) that determine whether it applies to a given arrangement.

expectedJSON.body: Before filing a civil action against a client employer for violations covered by Section 2810.3, a worker or the worker's representative must, at least 30 days beforehand, notify the client employer of the violations described in subdivision (b) (the wage-payment and workers' compensation coverage provisions). Neither the client employer nor the labor contractor may take adverse action against a worker for providing that notification or for filing a claim or civil action. Separately, upon request by a state enforcement agency or department, a client employer or labor contractor must provide the agency or department with information within its possession, custody, or control that is required to verify compliance with applicable state laws, and must make records available promptly for inspection and copying. The statute authorizes the Labor Commissioner, the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, and the Employment Development Department each to adopt regulations and rules of practice and procedure to administer and enforce the provisions within their respective jurisdictions.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, 30-day pre-filing notice requirement
citations.quote: At least 30 days prior to filing a civil action against a client employer for violations covered by this section, a worker or the worker’s representative shall notify the client employer of violations under subdivision (b).

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(e) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, anti-retaliation provision
citations.quote: Neither the client employer nor the labor contractor may take any adverse action against any worker for providing notification of violations or filing a claim or civil action.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(i) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, information requests by state enforcement agencies
citations.quote: Upon request by a state enforcement agency or department, a client employer or a labor contractor shall provide to the agency or department any information within its possession, custody, or control required to verify compliance with applicable state laws.

expectedJSON.gap: These citations are to different subdivisions of the same statute (Section 2810.3) rather than independent sources. This clause does not describe any implementing regulations the Labor Commissioner, the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, or the Employment Development Department may have adopted under their respective enforcement authority, and does not address the required contents or method of the 30-day pre-filing notice.

expectedJSON.body: Section 2810.3 does not prohibit a client employer from establishing, exercising, or enforcing by contract any otherwise lawful remedies against a labor contractor for liability created by the labor contractor's acts, and it does not prohibit a labor contractor from doing the same against a client employer for liability created by the client employer's acts. This preserves the parties' ability to allocate responsibility between themselves by contract (for example, through indemnification provisions), separate from the liability-sharing the statute itself imposes toward workers. The statute also provides that a waiver of Section 2810.3 is contrary to public policy and is void and unenforceable.

citations.quote: This section does not prohibit a client employer from establishing, exercising, or enforcing by contract any otherwise lawful remedies against a labor contractor for liability created by acts of a labor contractor.

citations.cite: California Labor Code, labor contractor's contractual remedies against client employer preserved
citations.quote: This section does not prohibit a labor contractor from establishing, exercising, or enforcing by contract any otherwise lawful remedies against a client employer for liability created by acts of a client employer.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 2810.3(m) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Labor Code, anti-waiver provision
citations.quote: A waiver of this section is contrary to public policy, and is void and unenforceable.

expectedJSON.gap: These citations are to different subdivisions of the same statute (Section 2810.3) rather than independent sources. This clause states that the statute preserves the parties' ability to allocate responsibility between themselves by contract; it does not describe how any particular indemnification provision should be drafted or would be interpreted, and does not address whether a specific contractual term between a given client employer and labor contractor is enforceable.
